Front: Event ID 4625 repeated 50+ times from same IP in 2 minutes?
Back: Brute force attack. Event ID 4625 = failed logon (Windows Security Log). Multiple rapid failures from single source indicates password guessing. Exam trap: differentiate from dictionary attack (uses common password list vs sequential attempts).

Front: Event ID 4624 followed immediately by 4672 (special privilege assigned)?
Back: Successful logon with admin privileges escalation. 4624 = successful logon. 4672 = admin privileges assigned to new logon. If from unusual source IP or off-hours, indicates compromise.

Front: Event ID 4688: svchost.exe spawning powershell.exe with encoded command?
Back: Lateral movement / malware execution. 4688 = process creation. svchost should NOT spawn PowerShell. Encoded (-EncodedCommand) is typical of Cobalt Strike / attacker tooling.

Front: Event ID 5156 repeated: outbound connections from workstation to unknown IP port 4444?
Back: C2 beaconing / reverse shell. 5156 = Windows Filtering Platform connection allowed. Outbound to high port (4444 common for Metasploit) indicates command & control channel.

Front: Event ID 7045: Service installed (sc.exe create WinUpdate) at 3 AM?
Back: Persistence mechanism. 7045 = new service installed. Malware often installs as service named to mimic legitimate Windows services. Run key, scheduled tasks also common persistence.

Front: Event ID 4740: Account locked out 3 times in 1 hour from 3 different source IPs?
Back: Password spray attack. Account lockout from multiple sources = distributed guessing to avoid lockout threshold on single source. Attackers rotate IPs to evade detection.

Front: Event ID 1102: Security log cleared at 2 AM?
Back: Evidence of cover-up. Attackers clear logs to hide activity. 1102 = audit log was cleared. Immediate investigation required — attacker likely already established persistence.

Front: DNS query to 16-character random string .com every 60 seconds with 20% jitter?
Back: DGA beaconing. Domain Generation Algorithm creates pseudorandom domains per epoch. Malware resolves to find C2 IP. Jitter (randomized interval) evades regular-interval detection.

Front: DNS TXT query to known malicious domain oversized response?
Back: DNS tunneling / data exfiltration. Data encoded in TXT record queries/responses. Bypasses firewalls since DNS is usually allowed. Detect by: unusual TXT query volume, oversized responses.

Front: HTTP GET to /etc/passwd returning 200 with file contents?
Back: Directory traversal success. ../.. sequences to escape web root. Should return 403/404. If returns 200 with /etc/passwd content, web server is compromised — immediate isolation needed.

Front: HTTP POST to /search?q=<script>alert('xss')</script> with 'Referer: evil.com'?
Back: Reflected XSS. Attacker injects script in URL parameter. Script executed in victim's browser when server reflects input without sanitization. Referer indicates attacker-controlled site delivered the crafted link.

Front: 5,000 HTTP requests to /login.php from single IP in 10 seconds with random usernames?
Back: Credential stuffing. Automated login attempts using breached username/password lists. Different from brute force (sequential password attempts). Rate limiting + CAPTCHA mitigates.

Front: 'UNION SELECT * FROM users --' in URL parameter returning user table data?
Back: SQL injection success. Attacker manipulates database query via unsanitized input. UNION adds results from another table. Mitigated by parameterized queries (prepared statements), not escaping.

Front: Single HTTP request with 'User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0' to every common path (admin, wp-admin, .env)?
Back: Automated scanner / reconnaissance. Tools like Dirb, Gobuster, Nikto enumerate directories/files. Logs show sequential requests to common paths regardless of 404 responses.

Front: Outbound SMTP (port 25) from workstation to 25 different external mail servers in 1 minute?
Back: Spam bot / malicious relay. Workstation compromised and sending spam. Legitimate servers use port 587 (submission). Workstations should never send port-25 SMTP.

Front: Outbound HTTPS (443) to known-bad IP in country with no business relationship?
Back: C2 over encrypted channel. Malware using HTTPS to blend with normal traffic. Destination IP in sanctioned/embargoed country is strong indicator. Block by IP reputation / threat intel feeds.

Front: ICMP echo replies with payload size > 64 bytes and irregular data patterns?
Back: ICMP tunneling / covert channel. Data hidden in ICMP payload. Normal ping: 32-64 bytes. Oversized or variable-size ICMP with entropy indicates C2 or exfiltration over ICMP.

Front: Incomplete TCP handshakes (SYN → SYN-ACK, no final ACK) from thousands of unique IPs?
Back: SYN flood DDoS. Three-way handshake: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK. Attacker sends SYN but never ACKs. Server waits for ACK, exhausting connection table. Mitigate with SYN cookies.

Front: Single IP: 10 failed logins (SSH), then successful login at 3 AM, then 5 GB data transfer to external IP?
Back: Credential compromise + data exfiltration. Initial brute force succeeded. Attacker then exfiltrated data. Timeline: attack→access→exfil is classic intrusion pattern.

Front: NanoCore / AgentTesla / Remcos process running on workstation with outbound connections?
Back: RAT (Remote Access Trojan) infection. These are commodity malware with C2. AgentTesla = keylogger/stealer. Remcos = remote control. NanoCore = plugin-based RAT. All common on exam.

Front: PowerShell script downloaded from internet and executed via base64 encoded command?
Back: Living-off-the-land attack. Attacker uses built-in Windows tools (PowerShell, WMI, certutil) to download and execute payload. No malware file written to disk — memory-only.

Front: Process: wscript.exe or cscript.exe running with child process: powershell.exe?
Back: Macro-based malware. VBScript/JavaScript (wscript/cscript) downloads or runs PowerShell payload. Common phishing attachment pattern. EDR detects parent-child anomaly.

Front: USB device insertion followed by immediate execution of random-named .exe?
Back: Baiting / USB drop attack. Attacker leaves infected USB drive. Autorun or user clicks malicious file. Mitigate: disable autorun, use GPO to block USB execution, endpoint protection.

Front: Network share (.csv or .xlsx) accessed by non-HR user at 2 AM, then external upload?
Back: Insider threat / data theft. User accessing data outside job scope + off-hours + external upload = exfiltration. DLP should detect large outbound transfers of sensitive file types.

Front: Event ID 4688: reg.exe add HKLM\...\Run /v恶意 /t REG_SZ...?
Back: Registry persistence (Run key). Malware adds entry to registry Run key so it executes at every boot. Common persistence locations: HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run, RunOnce.

Front: Event ID 4698: Scheduled task created to run .exe from AppData\Roaming?
Back: Scheduled task persistence. 4698 = scheduled task created. Tasks in AppData\Roaming = unusual. Legitimate tasks run from System32 or Program Files.

Front: Wireshark: ARP replies claiming 192.168.1.1 MAC is aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff (not actual gateway MAC)?
Back: ARP spoofing / MITM. Attacker sends fake ARP replies, associating their MAC with gateway IP. Victim traffic routed through attacker. Mitigate: Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) on switches.

Front: Nmap scan results: ports 22, 80, 443, 3306, 3389 open on public IP?
Back: Attack surface enumeration. These ports indicate SSH, HTTP, HTTPS, MySQL, RDP — common targets. Web server: expected 80/443. RDP (3389) open to internet = high risk.

Front: User reports fake login page at 'cornpany-login.com' that looks like company portal 'company-login.com'?
Back: Typosquatting / phishing infrastructure. Attacker registered lookalike domain. Common technique: swap letters, add hyphens, use different TLD (.net vs .com). Users enter creds → stolen.

Front: SMTP headers show 'Received: from [185.220.101.23]' but DKIM-Signature fails validation?
Back: Email spoofing / phishing. DKIM failure means email claims to be from your domain but digital signature doesn't match. SPF + DKIM + DMARC (p=reject) prevents spoofing.

Front: File downloaded: 'Invoice.pdf.exe' from email attachment?
Back: Malicious attachment. Double extension tricks Windows (hides .exe if 'Hide extensions for known file types' enabled). User sees Invoice.pdf, actually runs .exe. Block EXE in email gateway.

Front: User receives SMS: 'Your package is delayed, track here: bit.ly/3xK9mZ2'?
Back: Smishing (SMS phishing). Shortened URL hides malicious destination. Social engineering: urgency + package tracking is common pretext.

Front: Call to help desk: 'I'm VP Smith, I forgot my password, please reset and read me the new one'?
Back: Pretexting / vishing. Attacker impersonates executive to manipulate help desk. Verify identity through separate channel before making changes. Call-back to known number.

Front: Employee brings personal USB drive to workstation, plugs in, files start encrypting with .locked extension?
Back: Baiting + ransomware. USB drop infected workstation. Ransomware encrypts local + mapped drives. First step: isolate workstation from network immediately.

Front: Logs show user logged in from New York (US) at 9:00 AM and Tokyo (JP) at 9:15 AM same day?
Back: Impossible travel. User physically cannot be in both cities in 15 minutes. Indicates credential compromise — legitimate user + attacker both active. Reset credentials, revoke sessions.

Front: Firewall log: ALLOW 10.0.1.50:54321 → 203.0.113.88:445 (SMB) from non-file-server?
Back: Lateral movement over SMB. Internal host connecting to external IP on port 445 (SMB) is abnormal. WannaCry/EternalBlue spread using SMBv1 vulnerability. Block SMB outbound (445) at perimeter.

Front: System performance slow, 99% disk activity on C:\, many files renamed to .crypted extension?
Back: Ransomware in progress. File encryption + extension rename is signature of ransomware (e.g., .crypted, .encrypted, .lockbit). Immediate containment: isolate from network, disconnect storage.

Front: Web server log: %00 in URL parameter returning truncated response?
Back: Null byte injection (%00 = null). Older languages (C, Perl) treat null as string terminator. Attacker bypasses file extension checks: file.php%00.jpg passes as .jpg but executes as .php.

Front: Event ID 4670: Permissions on lsass.exe modified by process not named lsass.exe?
Back: Credential dumping / LSASS access. 4670 = permissions modified. LSASS stores Windows credentials in memory. Mimikatz / similar tools access LSASS to dump hashes. EDR alerts on LSASS access.

Front: Network flow: internal server → external IP on port 53 (DNS) with 500 KB/s sustained transfer?
Back: DNS tunneling / data exfiltration. DNS normally has small query/response sizes (avg ~100 bytes). Sustained high throughput over DNS indicates tunneling tool.

Front: User receives email with 'Dear [Name], click here to verify your account' linking to identical-looking login page?
Back: Spear phishing. Targeted attack on specific individual. Email personalized with recipient name. Landing page clones legitimate site. More convincing than generic phishing.

Front: E-mail headers: SPF = fail, DKIM = none, DMARC = none. Email purportedly from CEO requesting wire transfer?
Back: CEO fraud / business email compromise (BEC). No email authentication means anyone can spoof the domain. BEC = social engineering requesting wire transfer, gift cards, or sensitive data.

Front: SIEM alert: 25 failed logins (Event 4625) from different usernames, single IP, all using 'Winter2026!' password?
Back: Password spray attack. Single password tried against many accounts. Avoids account lockout (which triggers on per-user failures). Detect by: same password hash across multiple failed logons.

Front: Event ID 4656: Handle to SAM registry hive requested by non-SYSTEM process?
Back: SAM hive access attempt. SAM (Security Account Manager) stores local password hashes. Only SYSTEM should access the SAM hive. Process requesting handle is likely credential dumping tool.

Front: Linux auth.log: Failed password for root from 185.130.5.1 port 22 ssh2 repeated 1000 times?
Back: SSH brute force. Linux servers exposed to internet get constant SSH brute force. Mitigate: disable root SSH login, use key-based auth, fail2ban, change default port.

Front: Windows Defender alert: 'Trojan:Win32/Wacatac.B!ml' detected in Downloads folder?
Back: Trojan download. User downloaded and saved malware to Downloads folder. Wacatac = info-stealer trojan. ML tag = machine learning detection. Malware likely delivered via browser drive-by download.

Front: Process tree: Outlook.exe → cmd.exe → powershell.exe → rundll32.exe → regsvr32.exe?
Back: Office macro → LOLBins chain. Attacker uses Living-off-the-Land Binaries (LOLBins): cmd, PowerShell, rundll32, regsvr32, mshta, certutil. Each is legitimate but abused.

Front: Outbound HTTP request to pastebin.com from server containing base64-encoded data?
Back: Data staging / exfiltration. Pastebin used as dead-drop resolver or exfil destination. Base64 encoding is basic obfuscation (easily decoded). DLP should detect and block.

Front: Event ID 4719: Windows Firewall rule modified to allow inbound 3389 from any?
Back: Defense evasion. Attacker modifies firewall to enable RDP for persistence/access. 4719 = firewall rule changed. Monitor for unauthorized firewall rule additions.

Front: MFT examination: file created/modified timestamps show 2000-01-01 for malware.exe?
Back: Timestamping / anti-forensic. Attacker sets file timestamps to false date to evade timeline analysis. Timestamp anomalies in MFT (Master File Table) indicate deliberate manipulation.

Front: System has 2 administrator accounts: built-in Administrator + 'Admin_backup' created 3 days ago?
Back: Backdoor account. Attacker creates hidden admin account for persistence. Named to blend in. Exam trap: audit user accounts regularly, disable unused accounts, monitor new account creation (Event 4720).

Front: Memory dump of lsass.exe shows cleartext credentials?
Back: Credential dumping succeeded. Tools like Mimikatz extract passwords from LSASS memory. Mitigate: enable Credential Guard (virtualization-based security), LSA protection, Windows Defender Credential Guard.

Front: Scheduled task 'WindowsUpdate' runs daily at 2 AM but path is C:\Users\Public\update.exe?
Back: Fake scheduled task for persistence. Legitimate Windows Update is a service, not a task in Users\Public. Malware named to look like system task. Compare with legit task path (System32).

Front: 1000+ HTTP 404 errors for /wp-admin, /admin, /.env from single IP in 2 minutes?
Back: Web enumeration / reconnaissance. Automated tool probing for admin interfaces, config files, and known vulnerable paths. 404s mean server correctly blocked, but indicates active scanning.

Front: User credentials submitted to http://fake-login.company.com (not https) — credentials visible on network?
Back: Credential harvesting over HTTP. Fake login page served over HTTP (no padlock). Credentials sent in clear text. Even careful users may not notice HTTP vs HTTPS. Phishing awareness training.
